hints: Think about what happens to the principal quantum number of the outer electrons as you move from Be to Ra.
Consider how extra inner shells affect the pull felt by the outer electrons from the nucleus.
walkthrough:
Picture adding a new shell each time**
Imagine building the atoms from Be down to Ra. Each step down adds a whole new principal shell. So the outer electrons sit in n = 2, then 3, then 4, and so on. That alone puts the outer edge further from the nucleus.

See why attraction gets weaker**
More inner shells means more shielding. The inner electrons repel and block the nuclear charge. Even though proton number rises, the effective pull on the outer electrons falls because they are further away and better shielded. Weaker pull lets the electron cloud expand, so both atomic and ionic radii increase.

Final answer: Down the group an extra electron shell is added for each new period.
Increased distance and increased shielding reduce the attraction of the nucleus for the outer electrons, so radii increase.

hints: Compare the size of a Group 2 atom with its 2+ ion and recall what is lost when the ion forms.
Think about how losing the whole outer shell and keeping the same nuclear charge changes the pull per electron.
walkthrough:
Spot which must be bigger**
A Group 2 atom like $\text{Mg}$ is $[\text{Ne}]3s^2$. Its ion $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is just $[\text{Ne}]$. The ion has lost the entire outer shell, so it must be much smaller. That tells you the higher values, about 0.11 to 0.22 $\text{nm}$, are the atoms and the lower values, about 0.03 to 0.14 $\text{nm}$, are the ions.

Explain the shrinkage**
Two things shrink the ion. First, one shell is gone completely. Second, the nuclear charge is unchanged but now acts on fewer electrons, so the proton to electron ratio is higher. Stronger effective attraction pulls the remaining shells in closer. That is why every ion point sits well below its atom.

Final answer: Upper line with dots is atomic radii, lower line with crosses is ionic radii, as atoms are larger than the corresponding ions.
The atom loses its two outer shell electrons to form $\text{M}^{2+}$, so the ion has one fewer shell and a greater effective nuclear charge pulling the remaining electrons in more strongly.

hints: Recall which Group 2 anion decomposes on strong heating to give a brown gas plus a white oxide residue.
walkthrough:
Link brown gas to nitrate**
A brown gas on heating is the classic sign of $\text{NO}_{2}$. Only nitrates, $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$, decompose this way to give $\text{NO}_{2}$ plus $\text{O}_{2}$ and leave a white metal oxide behind. Carbonates give colourless $\text{CO}_{2}$, hydroxides give water, so the anion in L must be nitrate.
Final answer: Nitrate / $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$

hints: Think about which Group 2 hydroxides are soluble enough to give $\text{M}^{2+}(aq)$ and which Group 2 sulfates are insoluble white precipitates.
walkthrough:
Use the dense white precipitate clue**
The colourless solution contains $\text{M(OH)}_{2}(aq)$, so it provides $\text{M}^{2+}(aq)$. Adding $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ gives a dense white precipitate of $\text{MSO}_{4}$. Only $\text{BaSO}_{4}$ and $\text{SrSO}_{4}$ are sufficiently insoluble to do this, while $\text{CaSO}_{4}$ is slightly soluble and $\text{MgSO}_{4}$ is soluble. So M is Ba or Sr, and the ionic equation simply combines the two ions to form the solid.
Final answer: M = Ba / barium OR Sr / strontium; $\text{Ba}^{2+} + \text{SO}_{4}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_{4}$ OR $\text{Sr}^{2+} + \text{SO}_{4}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{SrSO}_{4}$

hints: Combine the 2+ charge of M with the 1- charge of nitrate to work out the formula of L.
Recall the three products formed when a Group 2 nitrate is heated strongly.
walkthrough:
Build the formula**
M is $2+$ and nitrate is $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$, so you need two nitrates to balance: $\text{M(NO}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$. That gives $\text{Ba(NO}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$ or $\text{Sr(NO}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$.

Write the decomposition**
Group 2 nitrates always decompose to oxide + nitrogen dioxide + oxygen: $$2\text{M(NO}_{3}\text{)}_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{MO} + 4\text{NO}_{2} + \text{O}_{2}$$ Check balance: 2 M, 4 N and 12 O on each side. The white solid that dissolves to give $\text{M(OH)}_{2}$ is the $\text{MO}$, which reacts with water: $\text{MO} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{M(OH)}_{2}$.

Final answer: Formula: $\text{Ba(NO}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$ OR $\text{Sr(NO}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$
Equation: $2\text{Ba(NO}_{3}\text{)}_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{BaO} + 4\text{NO}_{2} + \text{O}_{2}$ OR $2\text{Sr(NO}_{3}\text{)}_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{SrO} + 4\text{NO}_{2} + \text{O}_{2}$

hints: For the hydroxide, focus only on the ions that actually change, $\text{H}^{+}$ from the acid and $\text{OH}^{-}$ from the base.
For the carbonate, remember the acid provides $\text{H}^{+}$ and the carbonate provides $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ to make $\text{CO}_{2}$ and water.
walkthrough:
Strip to spectator free form for hydroxide**
Soil acidity means $\text{H}^{+}(aq)$. Calcium hydroxide supplies $\text{OH}^{-}(aq)$. Calcium ions do nothing, they are spectators. Cancel them out and you are left with the core neutralisation: $$\text{H}^{+} + \text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$

Strip to spectator free form for carbonate**
Calcium carbonate supplies $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$. Again $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ is a spectator. Two $\text{H}^{+}$ ions are needed for one carbonate to make carbon dioxide and water: $$2\text{H}^{+} + \text{CO}_{3}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{CO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ This also removes acidity while releasing $\text{CO}_{2}$ gas.

Final answer: calcium hydroxide: $\text{H}^{+} + \text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$
calcium carbonate: $2\text{H}^{+} + \text{CO}_{3}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{CO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

hints: Compare the solubility in water of calcium hydroxide with that of calcium carbonate.
Think about what heavy rain does to a soluble solid spread on soil and how long each solid will remain effective.
walkthrough:
Compare solubilities**
Calcium hydroxide is sparingly soluble and dissolves enough to be washed through soil. Calcium carbonate is effectively insoluble in water. In AS terms, hydroxides become more soluble down Group 2 while carbonates become less soluble, and calcium carbonate is the insoluble one here.

Link to rainfall**
In high rainfall, a more soluble base is quickly leached away and its neutralising effect is lost. Insoluble $\text{CaCO}_{3}$ stays in the topsoil, dissolving only slowly as acid arrives, so it gives long lasting neutralisation and needs less frequent reapplication.

Final answer: Calcium carbonate is insoluble / less soluble than calcium hydroxide.
It is less likely to be washed away / leached by rain so lasts longer in the soil.

hints: Recall the slow reaction of Mg with cold water that forms a hydroxide and hydrogen.
Recall that steam is hotter and drives the reaction further to form the oxide instead of the hydroxide.
walkthrough:
Cold water gives the hydroxide**
With cold water magnesium reacts very slowly: $$\text{Mg} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}$$ So the Mg containing product is magnesium hydroxide, $\text{Mg(OH)}_{2}$.

Steam gives the oxide**
With steam magnesium burns brightly and the hydroxide is not stable at that temperature. The product is magnesium oxide: $$\text{Mg} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{MgO} + \text{H}_{2}$$ So the Mg containing product is $\text{MgO}$.

Final answer: with cold water: $\text{Mg(OH)}_{2}$
with steam: $\text{MgO}$
